questions.question: When should you increase your following distance?

options.text: When traffic is light.
When traffic is heavy.
When you can see the roadway through vehicles in front of you.
When the weather is pleasant and clear.

questions.correctAnswerText: When traffic is heavy.
questions.explanation: Increase your following distance when conditions make it harder to stop quickly. This includes heavy traffic, poor weather, nighttime riding, or when you cannot see past the vehicle ahead.

questions.question: How do you swerve correctly?

options.text: Shift your weight quickly.
Turn the handlebars quickly.
Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.
Press the handgrip opposite the direction you want to turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn.
questions.explanation: To swerve, press the handgrip on the side where you want to turn. Press the opposite handgrip to return to your original direction once you are clear of the danger.

questions.question: What should you do to reduce your reaction time?

options.text: Ride slower than the speed limit.
Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes.
Shift into neutral when slowing down.
Pull in the clutch when turning.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes to reduce your reaction time. This is especially important in areas where hazards are likely.

questions.question: When choosing a helmet, which is NOT important?

options.text: It meets DOT safety standards.
It looks nice.
It fits snugly.
It has no defects.

questions.correctAnswerText: It looks nice.
questions.explanation: A good helmet must meet DOT standards, fit snugly all the way around, and have no defects like cracks, loose padding, or frayed straps. Appearance is not important for safety.

questions.question: In New Hampshire, when is a person age 21 or older considered legally intoxicated?

options.text: At 0.02 percent blood alcohol concentration (BAC).
At 0.04 percent blood alcohol concentration (BAC).
At 0.06 percent blood alcohol concentration (BAC).
At 0.08 percent blood alcohol concentration (BAC).

questions.correctAnswerText: At 0.08 percent blood alcohol concentration (BAC).
questions.explanation: A person age 21 or older with a BAC of 0.08 percent or higher is legally intoxicated. Riding a motorcycle while intoxicated is illegal and dangerous.

questions.question: What should you do if a driver is following you too closely?

options.text: Flash your brake light before you slow down to warn them.
Speed up.
Pull over to the side of the road.
Slow down.

questions.correctAnswerText: Flash your brake light before you slow down to warn them.
questions.explanation: Flash your brake light before slowing down to warn the tailgater. They may be watching you and not see hazards ahead that require traffic to slow.

questions.question: What should you do when a vehicle is passing you on your left?

options.text: Move as far to the right as possible to help them pass.
Move to the shoulder to help them pass.
Ride in the center of your lane.
Ride on the left side of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the center of your lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane when being passed. Moving toward the passing vehicle increases collision risk. Moving away might encourage them to merge back too soon. Stay centered for safety.

questions.question: If you cannot avoid hitting an object in the road, what should you do?

options.text: Speed up before hitting it.
Slow down before hitting it.
Lean the motorcycle.
Stay seated on the motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow down before hitting it.
questions.explanation: Slow down as much as you can before impact. Try to hit the object at a 90-degree angle. Keep your motorcycle upright, rise slightly off your seat, and ease off the throttle just before impact.

questions.question: What is the best lane position for a motorcycle?

options.text: The left side.
The center.
The right side.
There is no single best position.

questions.correctAnswerText: There is no single best position.
questions.explanation: No single lane position is always best. Change your position based on road and traffic conditions. Choose a position that gives you the most space and makes other drivers see you better.

questions.question: What is true about rounded, convex motorcycle mirrors?

options.text: They are easy to adjust to immediately.
They make cars look closer than they really are.
They show a narrow view of the road.
They make cars look farther away than they really are.

questions.correctAnswerText: They make cars look farther away than they really are.
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors show a wider view of the road behind you than flat mirrors. However, they make objects appear farther away than they actually are. Practice judging distances if you are not used to them.

questions.question: A rectangular sign can be a:

options.text: School crossing sign.
Railroad crossing sign.
Stop sign.
Speed limit sign.

questions.correctAnswerText: Speed limit sign.
questions.explanation: Speed limit signs are rectangular. They are white with black letters or symbols. These signs show road rules. You must follow them.

questions.question: When entering a highway or curve, motorcyclists riding in a group should:

options.text: Ride single-file.
Ride in a staggered formation.
Ride in pairs.
Ride in the far right portion of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride single-file.
questions.explanation: Staggered formation is usually best. However, switch to single-file when turning, taking curves, or entering or leaving a highway.

questions.question: The front brake provides about how much of a motorcycle's stopping power?

options.text: About 25 percent
About 50 percent
About 70 percent
About 95 percent

questions.correctAnswerText: About 70 percent
questions.explanation: The front brake is stronger than the rear brake. It provides at least 70 percent of the motorcycle's total stopping power.

questions.question: Making eye contact with other drivers:

options.text: Means that they see you.
Guarantees that they will yield to you.
Doesn't mean that they see you.
Is not worth the effort it takes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Doesn't mean that they see you.
questions.explanation: Do not rely on eye contact to know that a driver sees you. A driver may look directly at you but still not notice you.

questions.question: Face shields and goggles:

options.text: Will likely never need to be replaced.
Will develop scratches and become brittle, requiring regular replacement.
Should be made of breakable materials so they can break away in the event of a crash.
Should not allow air to pass through.

questions.correctAnswerText: Will develop scratches and become brittle, requiring regular replacement.
questions.explanation: Face shields and goggles are plastic. Over time, they get scratched and become brittle. Replace them often to stay protected and comfortable.

questions.question: If a dog is chasing your motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Swerve around the animal.
Stop until the animal loses interest.
Ride alongside the animal.
Approach the animal slowly, then speed up.

questions.correctAnswerText: Approach the animal slowly, then speed up.
questions.explanation: If a dog is chasing you, downshift and ride toward it slowly. Then accelerate quickly to leave it behind.

questions.question: When riding in a group, less experienced riders should ride:

options.text: In the front of the group.
Just behind the leader.
Close to the back of the group.
At the tail end of the group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Less experienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This way, they will not fall behind. Experienced riders behind them can watch and help if needed.

questions.question: To swerve, you should:

options.text: Turn the handlebars quickly.
Shift your weight quickly.
Press the handgrip in the direction of the turn.
Press the handgrip in the opposite direction of the turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip in the direction of the turn.
questions.explanation: To swerve, push the handgrip on the side where you want to go. To go left, push the left grip, then push the right to straighten. To go right, push the right grip, then the left.

questions.question: When making normal stops, you should:

options.text: Use only the rear brake.
Use only the front brake.
Use both the front and rear brakes.
Alternate between the front and rear brakes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both the front and rear brakes.
questions.explanation: Always use both brakes when slowing or stopping. Do this even for normal, everyday stops.

questions.question: Each traffic lane gives motorcyclists how many paths of travel?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

questions.correctAnswerText: Three
questions.explanation: Each lane has three paths for motorcyclists: the left, center, and right portions of the lane.

questions.question: What happens when you brake while turning a curve?

options.text: Use only the front brake.
It works the same as braking on a straight road.
You have more traction as you lean into the curve.
You may have less traction as you lean into the curve.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may have less traction as you lean into the curve.
questions.explanation: You can use both brakes while turning, but be very careful. When your motorcycle leans into a turn, your tires use some traction for turning. This leaves less traction for stopping.

questions.question: When passing parked cars, which part of your lane should you ride in?

options.text: The left portion of the lane
The center portion of the lane
The right portion of the lane
Either the left or right portion of the lane

questions.correctAnswerText: The left portion of the lane
questions.explanation: Ride in the left portion of your lane when passing parked cars. This keeps you away from opening car doors, people stepping out between cars, and cars pulling out of parking spaces.

questions.question: When it is raining, what should you do?

options.text: Ride in the center of the lane.
Pull off the road and wait for the rain to stop.
Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
Increase your speed.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: When rain first starts, the road is very slippery. Oil left by cars has not yet washed away. Ride in the tire tracks left by cars for better grip. The left tire track is usually your best choice.

questions.question: If one rider in a group wants to ride faster than the others, what should the group do?

options.text: Let the rider go ahead and meet at a set location later.
Speed up to match that rider's pace.
Split up so each rider can go their own speed.
Let the faster rider lead the group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Let the rider go ahead and meet at a set location later.
questions.explanation: If one rider wants to go faster, let them ride ahead of the group. Plan to meet at a set location later.

questions.question: When stopping, what should you do?

options.text: Grab at the front brake lever quickly.
Keep your knees against the gas tank and look ahead.
Apply increasing pressure to the rear brake only.
Use only the front brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your knees against the gas tank and look ahead.
questions.explanation: Apply the brakes smoothly and firmly. As your weight moves forward, the front wheel gets more traction. You can apply more front brake pressure while using less rear brake. Keep your knees against the gas tank and look ahead to stay in a straight line.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a good safety tip?

options.text: Slow down to a safe speed before turning.
Lean in the direction you want to turn.
Do not drag your feet on the road.
Avoid looking at other vehicles.

questions.correctAnswerText: Avoid looking at other vehicles.
questions.explanation: Slow down before turning and lean into the turn. Do not drag your feet, as they could catch on something and cause you to lose control. Always watch for other traffic.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an approved helmet type?

options.text: Full-face
One-quarter
One-half
Three-quarter

questions.correctAnswerText: One-quarter
questions.explanation: Approved helmets are one-half, three-quarter, or full-face types. A full-face helmet gives the best protection.

questions.question: If you must brake and swerve to avoid a hazard, what should you do?

options.text: Do one action, then the other.
Do both actions at the same time.
Always brake first, then swerve.
Only use the brakes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do one action, then the other.
questions.explanation: If you must brake and swerve, do one action first, then the other. Brake then swerve, or swerve then brake. Never do both at the same time.

questions.question: If your front wheel locks up, what should you do?

options.text: Continue holding the brake and the skid will stop.
Release the front brake and do not use it again.
Release the front brake and then quickly squeeze it again.
Release the front brake right away and apply it again smoothly.

questions.correctAnswerText: Release the front brake right away and apply it again smoothly.
questions.explanation: If your front wheel locks, release the front brake completely and right away. Then apply the brake again smoothly.

questions.question: Which vest or jacket color helps you be seen the most?

options.text: Red
Black
Silver
Blue

questions.correctAnswerText: Red
questions.explanation: Wear bright colors while riding to be more visible to others. Bright orange, yellow, red, or green work best. Avoid dark or dull colors.
